findings: For n=20, raw one-sided sign p<=0.05 requires k>=15 positives; p<=0.025 also k>=15; p<=0.0166667 requires k>=16; p<=0.0125 requires k>=16.

Therefore a four-test Holm PASS requires the two smallest raw p-values to come from tests with >=16/20 successes; the remaining two require >=15/20. Equivalently the minimal sorted success-count pattern is [16,16,15,15], total 62 successes across the four binary sign summaries.

The frozen >=70% CPSE_active>0 guard (>=14/20) is weaker than the active_gt_zero sign requirement whenever that test participates in a full Holm PASS: active_gt_zero must have at least 15/20, and may require 16/20 depending on its Holm rank. Thus the 70% guard is mathematically redundant for PASS, though still interpretable as an effect-description threshold.

The >=60% bidirectional guard (>=12/20 with delta_A>0 and delta_B>0) is NOT implied by CPSE_active sign positivity because CPSE_active=delta_A+delta_B can be positive with one directional component negative. It is independently constraining and useful against one-sided steering.

The mean-effect guards (mean CPSE_active>=0.10 and mean active-minus-each-control>=0.05) are not implied by sign counts: arbitrarily small positive values can satisfy sign tests. Conversely large positive effects on fewer families can satisfy the mean while failing sign tests. They are complementary, not contradictory.

No mathematical impossibility or internal contradiction was found in the frozen PASS rule. It is stringent: specificity requires at least 15/20 positive family advantages for every control comparison, with at least two of the four tests reaching 16/20 after Holm ordering, plus mean-effect and bidirectionality guards.
